chunks.text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is an architectural pattern that optimizes the output of a Large Language Model (LLM) by referencing an authoritative external knowledge base outside of its training data sources before generating a response. This reduces hallucinations.

Hybrid RAG combines dense vector representations (retrieving semantically similar items) with traditional BM25 keyword matching (relying on term frequencies). Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) combines these ranking scores to maximize precision.

Masal AI : FDE Assignment (Round 2)
Build a small AI-powered web app that helps a real-estate salesperson prioritize inbound leads and act
on them. One required feature is entirely up to you to invent, and we'll dig into your decisions together
in a 30-minute interview.
Role Context & What We're Testing
You'd be sitting between our product and real customers, configuring, demoing, and troubleshooting AI
voice systems live, often on a call with someone non-technical. That means two things both have to be
true: you can build working software quickly, and you can explain what you built clearly enough that a
buyer trusts it.
This assignment tests both:
• Building — can you turn an ambiguous brief into a working product in a few hours, using an AI
model as a real product component rather than a demo gimmick.
• Explaining — in your README, your 3-minute demo, and a live 30-minute interview where you'll
walk us through your own code.
The Assignment
Scenario. A real-estate sales team receives hundreds of leads a day. A salesperson needs to quickly see
which leads matter, what the customer actually wants, and what to do next.
Core requirements (all required)
1. Lead intake — a form to enter Name, Location, Property requirement, Budget, Buying timeline,
and a free-text Customer message (e.g. an inquiry or chat transcript).
2. AI analysis — call an AI model to generate: Lead summary, Customer intent, Key requirements,
Objections/concerns, Recommended next action, and a Suggested response to the customer.
3. Conversational interface — the salesperson can ask follow-up questions about a lead ("what
should I emphasize on the call?", "make my reply more assertive") and get answers grounded in
that lead's context, not a generic chatbot.
4. Lead list & prioritization (required). Don't build only a single-lead form. Support multiple saved
leads , in-memory or a real database, your call , each showing its AI analysis, and rank or group
them by some notion of priority or quality your AI analysis produces (a lead score, a
hot/warm/cold tag, an urgency flag , you decide).
5. Clear display — a salesperson should be able to scan the AI output in seconds.
Your own feature (required — content is up to you)
Add at least one feature you believe would genuinely help a salesperson in this workflow. We're
intentionally not specifying it. Think about what happens before, during, and after this screen in a real
salesperson's day.

Technical requirements
• At least one real AI API/model call , not a hardcoded or canned response.
• Deployed at a live URL we can open and test with no setup.
• A public GitHub repository.
• Free-tier resources only (Gemini API, Groq, OpenRouter, Hugging Face, Ollama locally, Vercel,
Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, GitHub Pages, or an equivalent).
• AI coding assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, Copilot, etc.) are expected, but you must
understand and be able to explain every part of what you submit.
Submission Requirements
Submit all four:
1. GitHub repository (public), with a README covering: what you built, an architecture overview,
which AI model/API you used and how it's called, how to run it locally, key technical decisions,
known limitations.
2. Live URL we can open and test without setup.
3. Demo video, max 3 minutes, screen-recorded, showing: the product, the main workflow end to
end, your own added feature, and one interesting technical or product decision you'd want to
discuss. Loom, Google Drive, or an unlisted YouTube link all work.
4. AI usage disclosure — which AI tools you used and for what (e.g. "Claude for prompt design and
the initial React scaffold, Copilot for autocomplete, ChatGPT to debug a CORS issue").
How to submit: A google form link will be shared with you.make sure all live links shared on the form
are open for anyone with link.

ContextRAG
B.Tech Final Year Project — Progress Report
1. Project Overview
ContextRAG (RAG Studio) is a context-aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) platform for enterprise
knowledge. Users upload documents (PDF, DOCX, TXT, Markdown or images) and ask questions in a chat. The
system finds the relevant parts of the documents and the language model answers only from that evidence,
with citations that show the sources.
The current version includes document ingestion with OCR, chunking, embeddings, a Qdrant vector database,
hybrid retrieval (semantic search plus BM25 keyword search), an LLM-based answer generation layer,
authentication, multi-session chat, a React web interface and an admin console for monitoring, analytics and
system configuration.
The proposed ContextRAG goes one step further. It adds a knowledge graph of entities and relationships as a
third retrieval source, and uses conversation history to make follow-up questions clear before retrieval.
Evidence from semantic, keyword and graph retrieval is fused, re-ranked and passed to the LLM for a
grounded, traceable answer. The project will also measure whether the graph improves results.
2. Problem Statement
Language models can give fluent answers that are wrong, out of date or not linked to any source. RAG reduces
this by giving the model evidence from the organization's own documents, but many document question-
answering systems still have clear weaknesses:
• semantic search alone can miss exact terms such as codes, names and identifiers, while keyword search
alone misses meaning.
• neither captures how entities and facts are related across different chunks or documents, so
relationship-type questions are answered poorly.
• follow-up questions such as "What are its advantages?" lose their meaning when the earlier
conversation is ignored.
• splitting documents into chunks can lose useful surrounding context, and scanned files need OCR.
• answers are often shown without clear sources, making them hard to verify.
• an enterprise system also needs secure access, multiple user sessions, and tools to monitor and
configure the system.
The problem addressed by this project is how to build one practical, working platform that combines context-
aware query handling, three-way retrieval (semantic, keyword and graph), evidence fusion, re-ranking and
source-grounded generation, and then to measure whether the added graph retrieval gives better retrieval
and answer quality than dense, BM25 or hybrid retrieval alone.
3. Project Objectives
The main objective is to build and evaluate a context-aware, graph-enhanced RAG platform that gives
accurate, grounded and traceable answers from enterprise documents. The specific objectives are:
• Build a practical document-based question-answering system using RAG that accepts common
document formats and supports OCR for image-based inputs.
• Split documents into context-aware chunks with metadata, create embeddings and store them in the
Qdrant vector database.

-- 1 of 12 --

• Combine dense semantic retrieval with BM25 keyword retrieval (hybrid retrieval).
• Use conversation history to rewrite follow-up questions into clear stand-alone queries before retrieval.
• Build a knowledge graph of entities and relationships from the documents and add graph retrieval as a
third retrieval source (proposed).
• Fuse the evidence from all retrievers and re-rank it with a cross-encoder before sending a compact
context to the LLM.
• Generate answers grounded in the retrieved evidence, with citations and source traceability.
• Provide authentication, document management and multi-session chat.
• Provide an admin console for service monitoring, analytics and system configuration.
• Evaluate the system by comparing Dense, BM25, Hybrid and Hybrid + Graph retrieval on retrieval
quality, answer quality, citation support and latency (planned).

8. Implementation Details
8.1 Backend and API layer
The FastAPI backend has separate routes for authentication, documents, chat and search. Configuration is
environment-driven. It connects the frontend, the stored metadata and the RAG services.
8.2 Document ingestion
Uploaded files are loaded according to their type; image-based documents go through OCR fallback. A
background ingestion task then performs chunking, embedding, vector storage, BM25 index update and
document-status update.
8.3 Retrieval
Retrieval is hybrid. Dense vector search in Qdrant finds text with similar meaning, while BM25 finds exact
terms such as identifiers, error codes and product names. The two result lists are merged with fusion logic to
give one candidate list.

-- 6 of 12 --

8.4 Context selection and reranking
The design takes a broad first-stage candidate set (Top-K is configurable in the admin console; the current
default is 10), re-ranks it with a cross-encoder and passes only the most relevant chunks to the LLM. A shorter,
more relevant context helps the model use the evidence better.
8.5 Grounded answer generation
Retrieved chunks are given to the LLM together with their source metadata, and the answer is returned with
source information so users can verify it.
8.6 Frontend
A React + Vite interface supports user login, document upload and chat, and talks to the backend through an
API client. The chat page has a New Chat button, searchable chat history, a paperclip button to attach
documents, a voice input button, a settings button and a Show Retrieval Diagnostics option; citations appear
below each answer.
8.7 Admin console
A System Administrator can open an admin console with seven tabs: Service Monitoring, Analytics Overview,
Users & Organization, Knowledge Base, System Config, Prompts Console and Observability Logs. Analytics
show usage figures and charts; System Config lets the administrator change models, chunking, Top-K,
temperature and switch features such as hybrid BM25 retrieval, cross-encoder re-ranking, query
expansion/rewrite and AI guardrails.
8.8 Search and vector sandbox
A search page lets users test retrieval directly: choose Semantic, BM25 or Hybrid (Reciprocal Rank Fusion),
select the distance metric (Cosine, Dot, L2), set a minimum similarity cutoff and number of results (K), and try
chunk segmentation on sample text. This helps tune and explain the retrieval behaviour.

13. Proposed Indexing Pipeline
Document → OCR / Parsing → Context-aware Chunking → Vector Index + BM25 Index + Knowledge Graph
• Parsing: Uploaded documents are loaded by type; scanned or image-based files go through OCR.
• Context-aware chunking: text is split into chunks that keep metadata and surrounding context
(document, section, position).
• Vector index: each chunk is embedded and stored in Qdrant for semantic search (implemented).
• BM25 index: each chunk is added to the keyword index for exact-term search (implemented).
• Knowledge graph: entities (people, systems, products, terms) and the relationships between them are
extracted from the chunks and stored, linked back to their source chunks (proposed).
14. Proposed Query Pipeline
Query + conversation history → 3-way retrieval → fusion → reranking → generation
• Query processing: the question and the session history are combined into a stand-alone retrieval query.
• Three-way retrieval: dense (Qdrant), BM25 and graph retrieval run on the same query.
• Fusion: the three ranked evidence lists are merged into one candidate list using rank fusion.
• Reranking: a cross-encoder re-scores the candidates and keeps only the most relevant ones.
• Context construction: the selected chunks (and related graph facts) are arranged into a compact
context.

• Generation: the LLM answers only from this evidence and the answer is returned with citations and
sources.
15. Proposed Contribution / Novelty
The contribution of ContextRAG is at the level of the unified architecture. Dense retrieval, BM25, rank fusion,
reranking and knowledge graphs are established techniques; the project combines them in one working
enterprise application and tests whether graph-enhanced retrieval improves results.
• Context-aware retrieval: conversation history is used to rewrite follow-up questions before retrieval.
• Three-way retrieval: semantic, keyword and graph evidence are retrieved together for every question.
• Graph-enhanced context: entities and relationships add connections between facts that plain chunk
similarity can miss.
• Evidence fusion + reranking: results from all retrievers are merged and re-scored so the best evidence
reaches the LLM.
• Grounded and traceable generation: answers use only retrieved evidence and show their sources.
• Unified architecture: document processing, retrieval, generation, chat, authentication and an admin
console work as one system.
The benefit of the graph component will be claimed only after the evaluation in Section 16 shows it.

18. Conclusion
Progress so far
ContextRAG has reached a meaningful working stage. A FastAPI backend, authentication, document upload
and management, ingestion with OCR support, chunking, embeddings, Qdrant vector storage, BM25 and
hybrid retrieval, a RAG answer pipeline with citations, persistent multi-session chat, a React frontend and an
admin console (monitoring, analytics, system configuration and a search sandbox) are in place. Together they
form a usable document-centric RAG application.
Some parts are built but still need validation: OCR on real scanned files, cross-encoder re-ranking, query
rewriting, AI guardrails and live data in the monitoring dashboards. Testing these end-to-end is the first
priority of the next stage.
Proposed project direction
The proposed ContextRAG extends the current hybrid system into a graph-enhanced, three-way retrieval
architecture. Each question will use conversation history, then retrieve evidence by meaning (Qdrant), by
exact terms (BM25) and by entity relationships (knowledge graph). The evidence is then fused, re-ranked by a
cross-encoder, built into a compact context and passed to the LLM for a grounded answer with citations and
source traceability.
The contribution claimed is the unified architecture that combines these established techniques in one
working enterprise application. Whether graph-enhanced retrieval gives a real benefit will be shown by the

evaluation plan, which compares Dense, BM25, Hybrid and Hybrid + Graph on retrieval quality, answer quality,
citation support and latency.
Next steps
• Short term: validate and test the existing pipeline end-to-end and verify the admin dashboards.
• Main development: design the graph schema, extract entities and relationships, build the graph, add
graph retrieval and integrate it with Qdrant and BM25.
• Final stage: run the evaluation, record the results, and prepare the final demonstration and report.

ContextRAG — Literature Review
LITERATURE REVIEW
ContextRAG: A Context-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation Platform for Enterprise Knowledge
B.Tech Final Year Project
1.1 Introduction
Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used as the core reasoning engine of modern software
systems, but they are fundamentally parametric: all their knowledge is encoded in trained weights at
the time of pretraining. This causes three well-documented problems — hallucination (fluent but
factually incorrect output), knowledge staleness (no awareness of information created after the training
cut-off), and poor traceability (no way to identify which source an answer came from). Retrieval-
Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses these limitations by coupling an LLM with a non-parametric
external knowledge source, so that relevant evidence can be retrieved at inference time and supplied to
the model as context. The foundational formulation of this idea was introduced by Lewis et al. [1], and
subsequent research has refined nearly every stage of the pipeline — retrieval, query understanding,
context selection, reranking, and evaluation.
Most published RAG research, however, addresses individual pipeline components in isolation, typically
on open-domain benchmarks such as Natural Questions or TriviaQA. Comparatively little work
integrates conversational context handling, hybrid (semantic + lexical) retrieval, reranking, careful
context selection, and source-grounded generation into a single enterprise-oriented platform, together
with operational concerns such as latency and session management. This gap motivates the present
project. ContextRAG is the proposed context-aware RAG architecture that integrates these elements for
enterprise knowledge applications; it is an engineering synthesis of peer-reviewed research,
implemented using FastAPI, Qdrant, the BAAI BGE embedding/reranking models, and a locally hosted
LLM served through Ollama. The remainder of this chapter reviews the literature underpinning each
component.
1.2 Foundational Work: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Lewis et al. (2020) — Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks [1]. This
paper formally introduced RAG, combining a pre-trained sequence-to-sequence generator (BART) with a
dense-vector index of Wikipedia passages retrieved via Dense Passage Retrieval, trained end-to-end.
Two variants were compared — RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token — and both were shown to outperform
purely parametric baselines on open-domain QA, producing more specific and factually consistent text.
Its main limitation is dependence on retriever quality, and it does not address multi-turn dialogue,
hybrid retrieval, or citation generation. Relevance: This paper establishes the conceptual foundation of
ContextRAG — the separation of an external knowledge store from the generative LLM and the retrieve-
then-generate data flow — which ContextRAG extends with conversational context handling, hybrid
retrieval, and reranking.
1.3 Evolution of RAG: Survey Literature
Gao et al. (2023) — Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey [2]. This
survey organises RAG research into three progressive paradigms — Naive RAG, Advanced RAG, and

Modular RAG — and decomposes the pipeline into retrieval, augmentation, and generation stages,
cataloguing optimisation techniques for each. It finds that Naive RAG suffers from retrieval imprecision,
Advanced RAG adds query rewriting and reranking, and Modular RAG generalises the pipeline into
interchangeable components. Relevance: ContextRAG can be positioned as an instance of Modular RAG,
decomposing its own pipeline into document processing, embedding, hybrid retrieval, reranking,
context selection, and generation modules.
Huang and Huang (2024) — A Survey on Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation for LLMs [3]. This
survey offers a finer-grained, four-stage decomposition of the RAG pipeline — pre-retrieval, retrieval,
post-retrieval, and generation — and treats RAG evaluation as a distinct research area, highlighting
reranking and context compression as critical post-retrieval steps. Relevance: This four-stage view maps
directly onto ContextRAG: context-aware query processing (pre-retrieval), hybrid retrieval (retrieval),
BGE reranking (post-retrieval), and Ollama-based generation with citations (generation).
1.4 Dense Retrieval and Embeddings
Karpukhin et al. (2020) — Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain QA [4]. This paper introduced
Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR), a dual-encoder architecture that embeds questions and passages
independently and retrieves via approximate nearest-neighbour search. DPR was shown to substantially
outperform a strong BM25 sparse baseline on open-domain QA retrieval accuracy, though it is weaker
on rare or exact-match tokens — a limitation that directly motivates hybrid retrieval. Relevance: DPR's
embed-and-search paradigm is the conceptual ancestor of ContextRAG's semantic retrieval component,
implemented using the BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 encoder and the Qdrant vector database.
Xiao et al. (2023) — C-Pack: Packaged Resources to Advance General Chinese Embedding [5]. This
paper released the BGE (BAAI General Embedding) family of models along with benchmark and training-
data resources, including cross-encoder rerankers, achieving state-of-the-art results on standard
embedding benchmarks. Relevance: This is the origin publication of the actual pre-trained models used
in ContextRAG — the BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 embedding model for retrieval and BAAI/bge-reranker-
base for reranking — making it the only directly implemented (rather than conceptual) reference in this
review.
1.5 Conversational and Context-Aware Retrieval
A basic RAG pipeline assumes each query is self-contained, but in an enterprise chatbot setting, follow-
up queries are often context-dependent (e.g., "What are its advantages?" following a question about
Kubernetes). Conversational query reformulation rewrites such queries into a stand-alone form before
retrieval.
Mo et al. (2023) — ConvGQR: Generative Query Reformulation for Conversational Search [6].
ConvGQR combines a query-rewriting model with a query-expansion model that generates a plausible
answer as additional retrieval context, aligning the reformulation objective with retrieval effectiveness
rather than merely mimicking human rewrites. It reports consistent retrieval-performance gains across
conversational search benchmarks, at the cost of added training complexity. Relevance: ConvGQR
grounds ContextRAG's principle of using conversation history to reformulate context-dependent queries
before retrieval, though ContextRAG does not implement its specific dual rewrite-and-expansion
architecture.

Jang et al. (2024) — IterCQR: Iterative Conversational Query Reformulation with Retrieval Guidance
[7]. IterCQR iteratively trains a query-reformulation model using retrieval-similarity signals as reward,
removing the need for costly human-annotated rewrites, and reports strong generalisation to unseen
datasets and low-resource conditions. Relevance: It reinforces the design principle behind ContextRAG's
context-aware query-processing module, which is cited as related work rather than an implemented
training procedure.
1.6 Hybrid Retrieval
Dense retrieval excels at semantically related but lexically dissimilar matches, while sparse, term-based
retrieval remains effective for exact identifiers, codes, and product names. Hybrid retrieval combines
both signals.
Robertson and Zaragoza (2009) — The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond [12].
This monograph formalises the Probabilistic Relevance Framework underlying BM25 and its field-
weighted extension BM25F, explaining BM25's continued robustness as a lexical scoring function even in
the era of neural retrieval. Relevance: BM25 provides the theoretical basis for the keyword-retrieval
component of ContextRAG's hybrid module, important for enterprise documents containing exact error
codes and ticket numbers.
Cormack, Clarke, and Büttcher (2009) — Reciprocal Rank Fusion Outperforms Condorcet and
Individual Rank Learning Methods [13]. This paper proposes Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), an
unsupervised method that scores documents by summing reciprocal rank positions across ranked lists,
requiring no training or score calibration, and shown to consistently outperform individual retrievers
and Condorcet Fuse. Relevance: RRF provides ContextRAG's training-free approach for fusing the
semantic (Qdrant) and keyword (BM25) candidate lists before reranking.
1.7 Reranking
Khattab and Zaharia (2020) — ColBERT: Efficient and Effective Passage Search via Contextualized Late
Interaction over BERT [8]. ColBERT introduces a late-interaction architecture that encodes queries and
documents independently into token-level embeddings, applying a lightweight MaxSim operation at
scoring time, achieving cross-encoder-competitive ranking effectiveness at much lower query-time cost.
Relevance: ColBERT supports the general two-stage retrieve-then-rerank principle used in ContextRAG,
which instead applies the separately trained BAAI/bge-reranker-base cross-encoder to the merged
hybrid candidate set.
1.8 Long Context and Context Selection
Liu et al. (2024) — Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts [9]. This study finds
that model performance on long-context tasks follows a U-shaped curve: performance is highest when
relevant information appears at the very beginning or end of the context and degrades significantly
when it falls in the middle — the "lost in the middle" effect — even for models designed for long
contexts. Relevance: This finding directly justifies ContextRAG's narrowing of a broader first-stage Top-K
(20) to a smaller, reranked final context (5) via the BGE reranker, reducing the risk of relevant evidence
being buried mid-context.
1.9 Adaptive RAG

Asai et al. (2024) — Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
[10]. Self-RAG trains a single LLM to adaptively decide when retrieval is necessary and to generate
"reflection tokens" that critique the relevance and quality of retrieved evidence and its own output,
significantly outperforming strong RAG baselines on QA and fact-verification tasks. Relevance: Self-RAG
is reviewed as a future direction rather than an implemented component — ContextRAG currently
always retrieves and always passes a reranked context to the LLM.
1.10 Graph-Based Context Retrieval for Code Generation (Related
Domain)
A separate line of RAG research addresses repository-level code generation, where the challenge is not
open-domain factual QA but retrieving the specific functions a target piece of code actually depends on.
This work is reviewed here as an adjacent domain that reinforces, from a different angle, the principle
that similarity-based retrieval alone is insufficient and that structural or complementary retrieval signals
improve grounding.
Liu et al. (2026) — Effective and Efficient Context Retrieval via Partial Dependency Graph for
Repository-Level Code Generation [14]. This paper proposes DyRetriever, which uses an LLM to
dynamically construct a partial code dependency graph on demand — selecting entry-point functions
from a target function's signature and then performing multi-hop reasoning to judge which dependent
functions are actually useful — rather than statically parsing a global repository graph with fixed rules.
Combined with similarity-based retrieval into a system called DyCoder, it reports relative Pass@1
improvements of 25.63% and 59.73% over RAG-based baselines on the CoderEval and DevEval
benchmarks respectively, while running 7.4× faster than static graph-construction baselines such as
RepoScope. Its scope is repository-level code generation rather than general enterprise document QA,
so it does not address conversational reformulation, hybrid lexical/semantic retrieval, or citation
grounding. Relevance: This paper illustrates a retrieval paradigm complementary to ContextRAG's —
LLM-driven, on-demand structural retrieval rather than embedding-based semantic retrieval — and
supports the broader case, echoed by DPR [4] and BM25 [12] on hybridising retrieval signals, that
combining structurally-aware and similarity-based retrieval outperforms either alone. It is reviewed as a
related direction rather than an implemented component, since ContextRAG's chunking and retrieval
remain content-based rather than dependency-graph-based.
1.11 Hallucination, Grounding, and Citations
A central motivation for RAG is that grounding generation in retrieved evidence reduces hallucination.
Building on this shared understanding across the literature reviewed above, ContextRAG treats
grounding and citation as first-class design goals: the generation prompt explicitly presents retrieved
chunks with source metadata, the LLM is instructed to answer only from supplied evidence, and the
returned answer includes source-document identifiers, inline citations, and full retrieved-document
traceability.
1.12 RAG Evaluation
Ru et al. (2024) — RAGChecker: A Fine-grained Framework for Diagnosing Retrieval-Augmented
Generation [11]. RAGChecker decomposes generated answers into individual claims and checks
entailment against retrieved evidence and reference answers, producing separate diagnostic metrics for

retrieval quality and generation faithfulness that correlate more strongly with human judgment than
prior coarse-grained metrics. Relevance: ContextRAG's performance-monitoring design — tracking
retrieval latency, generation latency, and retrieval confidence separately — mirrors RAGChecker's
separation of retrieval and generation concerns, though RAGChecker itself is not implemented at
runtime.

1.14 Research Gap
The literature shows RAG has matured along independent directions: dense retrieval [4,5],
conversational reformulation [6,7], hybrid retrieval [12,13], reranking [8,5], long-context management
[9], adaptive retrieval [10], and fine-grained evaluation [11]. It would be inaccurate to claim any single
component is unsolved. The gap this project addresses is one of integration: each paper contributes a
solution to one pipeline stage, typically demonstrated in isolation on open-domain academic
benchmarks. Comparatively little published work demonstrates a single, coherent, enterprise-oriented
platform that simultaneously combines conversational context handling, hybrid retrieval, cross-encoder
reranking, deliberate context selection, source-grounded generation with citations, and operational
performance monitoring — all deployed with practical concerns such as authentication and multi-
session conversation management.

Concurrent work on repository-level code generation, such as DyRetriever [14], similarly demonstrates
that structural, on-demand retrieval can outperform static or purely similarity-based methods —
reinforcing, in an adjacent domain, this project's premise that integrating complementary retrieval
signals yields gains beyond any single technique alone.
1.15 Proposed ContextRAG Architecture
The proposed architecture operates in two phases. In the indexing phase, enterprise documents are
uploaded through a FastAPI backend, text is extracted, documents are chunked with metadata, each
chunk is embedded using BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5, and vectors are stored in Qdrant. In the query phase,
the incoming query is combined with session conversation history; a context-aware query-processing
step (informed by ConvGQR [6] and IterCQR [7]) produces a stand-alone retrieval query; hybrid retrieval
(informed by BM25 [12], DPR [4], and RRF [13]) produces a broad candidate set; the BAAI/bge-reranker-
base cross-encoder [5] reorders these candidates; a smaller final context is selected in line with the long-
context findings of Liu et al. [9]; this context, together with the query and history, is passed to a locally
hosted LLM served through Ollama for grounded generation; and the answer is returned with citations,
source traceability, and logged performance metrics (retrieval latency, generation latency, retrieval
confidence), in the spirit of RAGChecker [11].
1.16 Literature Review Summary
This chapter traced the foundational RAG formulation [1] through its systematisation into Naive,
Advanced, and Modular paradigms [2,3], and reviewed the specific advances underpinning each stage of
a modern enterprise pipeline: dense semantic retrieval [4,5], lexical retrieval and rank fusion for hybrid
search [12,13], conversational query reformulation [6,7], late-interaction and cross-encoder reranking
[8,5], positional effects motivating context selection [9], adaptive/self-reflective retrieval as an emerging
direction [10], and fine-grained evaluation methodology [11]. It also reviewed, as a related domain,
LLM-driven structural retrieval for repository-level code generation [14], which reinforces the value of
combining complementary retrieval signals. Collectively, these establish that an effective enterprise RAG
platform requires context-aware query understanding, complementary retrieval signals, deliberate
candidate refinement, careful context budgeting, grounded generation, and continuous evaluation.
ContextRAG is presented as an engineering synthesis of these established directions — implemented
using FastAPI, Qdrant, the BAAI BGE embedding/reranking models, and Ollama — rather than a novel
algorithmic contribution to any single pipeline stage.

The proposed architecture operates in two phases. In the indexing phase, enterprise documents are
uploaded through a FastAPI backend, text is

the incoming query is combined with session conversation history; a context-aware

hosted LLM served through Ollama for grounded

ally

source traceability, and logged performance metrics (retrieval latency, generation latency, retrieval

1.16 Literature Review Summary
This chapter traced the foundational RAG formulation [1] through its systematisation into Naive,
Advanced, and Modular paradigms [2,3], and reviewed the specific advances underpinning each stage of
a modern enterprise pipeline: dense semantic retrieval [4,5],

terprise pipeline: dense semantic retrieval [4,5], lexical retrieval and rank fusion for hybrid
search [12,13], conversational query reformulation [6,7], late-interaction and cross-encoder reranking
[8,5], positional effects motivating context selection [9], adaptive/self-reflective retrieval as an

tion [9], adaptive/self-reflective retrieval as an emerging
direction [10], and fine-grained evaluation methodology [11]. It also reviewed, as a related domain,
LLM-driven structural retrieval for repository-level code generation [14], which reinforces the value of
combining complementary retrieval

ces the value of
combining complementary retrieval signals. Collectively, these establish that an effective enterprise RAG
platform requires context-aware query understanding, complementary retrieval signals, deliberate
candidate refinement, careful context budgeting, grounded generation, and

areful context budgeting, grounded generation, and continuous evaluation.
ContextRAG is presented as an engineering synthesis of these established directions — implemented
using FastAPI, Qdrant, the BAAI BGE embedding/reranking models, and Ollama — rather than a novel

details, dashboard and CSV.

meaningful employee details if the employee is later deleted.

CRUD APIs for Employees and Tasks (Add, Edit, Delete, View) with pagination.

Return proper errors: 400 invalid data or broken rule, 404 not found, 409 duplicate employee ID or email.

ContextRAG
B.Tech Final Year Project — Progress Report
1. Project Overview
ContextRAG (RAG Studio) is a context-aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) platform for enterprise
knowledge. Users upload documents (PDF, DOCX, TXT, Markdown or images) and ask questions in a chat. The
system finds the relevant parts of the documents and the language model answers only from that evidence,
with citations that show the sources.
The current version includes document ingestion with OCR, chunking, embeddings, a Qdrant vector database,
hybrid retrieval (semantic search plus BM25 keyword search), an LLM-based answer generation layer,
authentication, multi-session chat, a React web interface and an admin console for monitoring, analytics and
system configuration.
The proposed ContextRAG goes one step further. It adds a knowledge graph of entities and relationships as a
third retrieval source, and uses conversation history to make follow-up questions clear before retrieval.
Evidence from semantic, keyword and graph retrieval is fused, re-ranked and passed to the LLM for a
grounded, traceable answer. The project will also measure whether the graph improves results.
2. Problem Statement
Language models can give fluent answers that are wrong, out of date or not linked to any source. RAG reduces
this by giving the model evidence from the organization's own documents, but many document question-
answering systems still have clear weaknesses:
• semantic search alone can miss exact terms such as codes, names and identifiers, while keyword search
alone misses meaning.
• neither captures how entities and facts are related across different chunks or documents, so
relationship-type questions are answered poorly.
• follow-up questions such as "What are its advantages?" lose their meaning when the earlier
conversation is ignored.
• splitting documents into chunks can lose useful surrounding context, and scanned files need OCR.
• answers are often shown without clear sources, making them hard to verify.
• an enterprise system also needs secure access, multiple user sessions, and tools to monitor and
configure the system.
The problem addressed by this project is how to build one practical, working platform that combines context-
aware query handling, three-way retrieval (semantic, keyword and graph), evidence fusion, re-ranking and
source-grounded generation, and then to measure whether the added graph retrieval gives better retrieval
and answer quality than dense, BM25 or hybrid retrieval alone.
3. Project Objectives
The main objective is to build and evaluate a context-aware, graph-enhanced RAG platform that gives
accurate, grounded and traceable answers from enterprise documents. The specific objectives are:
• Build a practical document-based question-answering system using RAG that accepts common
document formats and supports OCR for image-based inputs.
• Split documents into context-aware chunks with metadata, create embeddings and store them in the
Qdrant vector database.

-- 1 of 12 --

• Combine dense semantic retrieval with BM25 keyword retrieval (hybrid retrieval).
• Use conversation history to rewrite follow-up questions into clear stand-alone queries before retrieval.
• Build a knowledge graph of entities and relationships from the documents and add graph retrieval as a
third retrieval source (proposed).
• Fuse the evidence from all retrievers and re-rank it with a cross-encoder before sending a compact
context to the LLM.
• Generate answers grounded in the retrieved evidence, with citations and source traceability.
• Provide authentication, document management and multi-session chat.
• Provide an admin console for service monitoring, analytics and system configuration.
• Evaluate the system by comparing Dense, BM25, Hybrid and Hybrid + Graph retrieval on retrieval
quality, answer quality, citation support and latency (planned).

8. Implementation Details
8.1 Backend and API layer
The FastAPI backend has separate routes for authentication, documents, chat and search. Configuration is
environment-driven. It connects the frontend, the stored metadata and the RAG services.
8.2 Document ingestion
Uploaded files are loaded according to their type; image-based documents go through OCR fallback. A
background ingestion task then performs chunking, embedding, vector storage, BM25 index update and
document-status update.
8.3 Retrieval
Retrieval is hybrid. Dense vector search in Qdrant finds text with similar meaning, while BM25 finds exact
terms such as identifiers, error codes and product names. The two result lists are merged with fusion logic to
give one candidate list.

-- 6 of 12 --

8.4 Context selection and reranking
The design takes a broad first-stage candidate set (Top-K is configurable in the admin console; the current
default is 10), re-ranks it with a cross-encoder and passes only the most relevant chunks to the LLM. A shorter,
more relevant context helps the model use the evidence better.
8.5 Grounded answer generation
Retrieved chunks are given to the LLM together with their source metadata, and the answer is returned with
source information so users can verify it.
8.6 Frontend
A React + Vite interface supports user login, document upload and chat, and talks to the backend through an
API client. The chat page has a New Chat button, searchable chat history, a paperclip button to attach
documents, a voice input button, a settings button and a Show Retrieval Diagnostics option; citations appear
below each answer.
8.7 Admin console
A System Administrator can open an admin console with seven tabs: Service Monitoring, Analytics Overview,
Users & Organization, Knowledge Base, System Config, Prompts Console and Observability Logs. Analytics
show usage figures and charts; System Config lets the administrator change models, chunking, Top-K,
temperature and switch features such as hybrid BM25 retrieval, cross-encoder re-ranking, query
expansion/rewrite and AI guardrails.
8.8 Search and vector sandbox
A search page lets users test retrieval directly: choose Semantic, BM25 or Hybrid (Reciprocal Rank Fusion),
select the distance metric (Cosine, Dot, L2), set a minimum similarity cutoff and number of results (K), and try
chunk segmentation on sample text. This helps tune and explain the retrieval behaviour.

13. Proposed Indexing Pipeline
Document → OCR / Parsing → Context-aware Chunking → Vector Index + BM25 Index + Knowledge Graph
• Parsing: Uploaded documents are loaded by type; scanned or image-based files go through OCR.
• Context-aware chunking: text is split into chunks that keep metadata and surrounding context
(document, section, position).
• Vector index: each chunk is embedded and stored in Qdrant for semantic search (implemented).
• BM25 index: each chunk is added to the keyword index for exact-term search (implemented).
• Knowledge graph: entities (people, systems, products, terms) and the relationships between them are
extracted from the chunks and stored, linked back to their source chunks (proposed).
14. Proposed Query Pipeline
Query + conversation history → 3-way retrieval → fusion → reranking → generation
• Query processing: the question and the session history are combined into a stand-alone retrieval query.
• Three-way retrieval: dense (Qdrant), BM25 and graph retrieval run on the same query.
• Fusion: the three ranked evidence lists are merged into one candidate list using rank fusion.
• Reranking: a cross-encoder re-scores the candidates and keeps only the most relevant ones.
• Context construction: the selected chunks (and related graph facts) are arranged into a compact
context.

• Generation: the LLM answers only from this evidence and the answer is returned with citations and
sources.
15. Proposed Contribution / Novelty
The contribution of ContextRAG is at the level of the unified architecture. Dense retrieval, BM25, rank fusion,
reranking and knowledge graphs are established techniques; the project combines them in one working
enterprise application and tests whether graph-enhanced retrieval improves results.
• Context-aware retrieval: conversation history is used to rewrite follow-up questions before retrieval.
• Three-way retrieval: semantic, keyword and graph evidence are retrieved together for every question.
• Graph-enhanced context: entities and relationships add connections between facts that plain chunk
similarity can miss.
• Evidence fusion + reranking: results from all retrievers are merged and re-scored so the best evidence
reaches the LLM.
• Grounded and traceable generation: answers use only retrieved evidence and show their sources.
• Unified architecture: document processing, retrieval, generation, chat, authentication and an admin
console work as one system.
The benefit of the graph component will be claimed only after the evaluation in Section 16 shows it.

18. Conclusion
Progress so far
ContextRAG has reached a meaningful working stage. A FastAPI backend, authentication, document upload
and management, ingestion with OCR support, chunking, embeddings, Qdrant vector storage, BM25 and
hybrid retrieval, a RAG answer pipeline with citations, persistent multi-session chat, a React frontend and an

form a usable document-centric RAG application.
Some parts are built but still need validation: OCR on real scanned files, cross-encoder re-ranking, query
rewriting, AI guardrails and live data in the monitoring dashboards. Testing these end-to-end is the first
priority of the next stage.
Proposed project direction
The proposed ContextRAG extends the current hybrid system into a graph-enhanced, three-way retrieval
architecture. Each question will use conversation history, then retrieve evidence by meaning (Qdrant), by
exact terms (BM25) and by entity relationships (knowledge graph). The evidence is then fused, re-ranked by a
cross-encoder, built into a compact context and passed to the LLM for a grounded answer with citations and
source traceability.
The contribution claimed is the unified architecture that combines these established techniques in one
working enterprise application. Whether graph-enhanced retrieval gives a real benefit will be shown by the
evaluation plan, which compares Dense, BM25, Hybrid and Hybrid + Graph on retrieval quality, answer quality,
citation support and latency.
Next steps
• Short term: validate and test the existing pipeline end-to-end and verify the admin dashboards.
• Main development: design the graph schema, extract entities and relationships, build the graph, add
graph retrieval and integrate it with Qdrant and BM25.
• Final stage: run the evaluation, record the results, and prepare the final demonstration and report.

8.3 Retrieval
Retrieval is hybrid. Dense vector search in Qdrant finds text with similar meaning, while BM25 finds exact
terms such as identifiers, error codes and product names. The two result

ers, error codes and product names. The two result lists are merged with fusion logic to
give one candidate list.

8.4 Context selection and reranking
The design takes a broad first-stage candidate set (Top-K is configurable in the admin console; the current
default is 10), re-ranks it with a cross-encoder and passes only the most relevant chunks to the LLM. A shorter,
more relevant context helps the model use

shorter,
more relevant context helps the model use the evidence better.
8.5 Grounded answer generation
Retrieved chunks are given to the LLM together with their source metadata, and the answer is returned with
source information so users can verify it.

14. Proposed Query Pipeline
Query + conversation history → 3-way retrieval → fusion → reranking →

n history → 3-way retrieval → fusion → reranking → generation
• Query processing: the question and the session history are combined into a stand-alone retrieval query.
• Three-way retrieval: dense (Qdrant), BM25 and graph retrieval run on the same query.
• Fusion: the three ranked evidence lists are

ery.
• Fusion: the three ranked evidence lists are merged into one candidate list using rank fusion.
• Reranking: a cross-encoder re-scores the candidates and keeps only the most relevant ones.
• Context construction: the selected chunks (and related graph facts) are arranged into a compact
context.

• Generation: the LLM answers only from this evidence and the answer is returned with citations and
sources.

Rohit Gurunath Sharma (born 30 April 1987) is an Indian international cricketer and the former captain of the India national cricket team in all formats of the game.[3] He is a right-handed top-order batter. He represents Mumbai in domestic cricket and Mumbai Indians in the Indian Premier League. Sharma was a member of the teams that won the 2007 T20 World Cup, the 2013 ICC Champions Trophy and was the winning captain of the 2024 T20 World Cup and the 2025 ICC Champions Trophy. Sharma is widely regarded as a modern-day great, known for his leadership and explosive batting.[4]

Sharma holds several batting records which include most sixes in international cricket,[a] most double centuries in ODI cricket (three), most centuries at Cricket World Cups (seven) and joint most centuries in Twenty20 Internationals (five).[6] He also holds the world record for the highest individual score (264) in a One Day International (ODI) and also holds the record for scoring most centuries (five) in a single Cricket World Cup, for which he won the ICC Men's ODI Cricketer of the Year award in 2019.[7] He is the first and only captain to lead a team in all[b] ICC tournament finals.[8]

He formerly captained Mumbai Indians and the team has won five Indian Premier League titles in 2013, 2015, 2017, 2019 and 2020 under him, making him the most successful captain in IPL history, sharing this record with MS Dhoni. He is also one of two players who have played in every edition of the T20 World Cup, from the inaugural edition in 2007 till 2024.[c] He is the only Indian player to win two T20 World Cups. He became the second Indian captain to win a T20 World Cup.

He has received three national honours, the Arjuna Award in 2015, the prestigious Khel Ratna Award in 2020 by the Government of India, and the Padma Shri, India's fourth-highest civilian award, in 2026, for his immense, long standing contribution to Indian cricket, which notably includes leading India to victory in the 2024 T20 World Cup[9][10][11] and the 2025 ICC Champions Trophy. Under his captaincy, India also won the 2018 Asia Cup and the 2023 Asia Cup, the seventh and eighth time the country won the title, both in ODI format as well as the 2018 Nidahas Trophy, their second overall and first in T20I format.

Early life
Sharma was born on 30 April 1987 into a Marathi-Telugu family in Bansod, Nagpur, Maharashtra, India.[12][13][3] His mother, Purnima Sharma, is from Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh.[14] His father, Gurunath Sharma, worked as a caretaker of a transport firm storehouse. Sharma was raised by his grandparents and uncles in Borivali because of his father's low income. He would visit his parents, who lived in a single-room house in Dombivli, only during weekends.[15] He has a younger brother, Vishal Sharma.[16]

Sharma joined a cricket camp in 1999 with his uncle's money. Dinesh Lad, his coach at the camp, asked him to change his school to Swami Vivekanand International School, where Lad was the coach and the cricket facilities were better than those at Sharma's old school. Sharma recollects, "I told him I couldn't afford it, but he got me a scholarship. So for four years I didn't pay a penny, and did well in my cricket".[16] Sharma started as an off-spinner who could bat a bit before Lad noticed his batting ability and promoted him from number eight to open the innings. He excelled in the Harris and Giles Shield school cricket tournaments, scoring a century on debut as an opener.[17]

Youth career
Sharma made his List A debut for West Zone against Central Zone in the Deodhar Trophy at Gwalior in March 2005. Batting at number eight, he scored 31 not out as West Zone won by 3 wickets with 24 balls remaining. Cheteshwar Pujara and Ravindra Jadeja made their debuts in the same match.[18] It was Sharma's unbeaten innings of 142 in 123 balls against North Zone at the Maharanna Bhupal College Ground in Udaipur in the same tournament that brought him into the limelight.[19] He visited Abu Dhabi and Australia with the India A squad and was then included among India's 30-member probable's list for the upcoming ICC Champions Trophy tournament, although he did not make the final squad.[20]

Sharma made his first-class debut for India A against New Zealand A at Darwin in July 2006. He scored 57 and 22 as India won by 3 wickets.[21] He made his Ranji Trophy debut for Mumbai in the 2006–07 season and scored 205 off 267 balls against Gujarat.[22] Mumbai went on to win the tournament with Sharma scoring a half-century (57) in his second innings in the final against Bengal.[23]

Sharma has spent his entire domestic first-class career at Mumbai. In December 2009, he made his highest career score of 309 not out in the Ranji Trophy against Gujarat.[24] In October 2013, upon the retirement of Ajit Agarkar, he was appointed team captain ahead of the 2013–14 season.[25]

Virat Kohli (born 5 November 1988) is an Indian international cricketer and former all-format captain of the Indian national cricket team. He is a right-handed batter and an occasional right-arm medium-pace bowler. Considered one of the greatest batters in cricket, he has been acclaimed for his batting skills and records. Kohli has the most centuries in ODIs and the second-most centuries in international cricket with 86 tons across all formats. He is also the leading run-scorer in the Indian Premier League.

Kohli was the captain of the 2008 U19 World Cup winning team and was a crucial member of the Indian teams that won 2011 Cricket World Cup, 2013 Champions Trophy, 2024 T20 World Cup, and 2025 Champions Trophy. He plays for Royal Challengers Bengaluru in the Indian Premier League and for Delhi in domestic cricket. In 2013, Kohli was ranked number one in the ODI batting rankings. In 2015, he achieved the same in T20I cricket. In 2018, he was ranked number one in Test cricket, making him the only Indian to hold the top spot in all three formats. He is the first player to score 20,000 international runs in a decade. He was the Cricketer of the Decade for 2011 to 2020.

Kohli has won ten ICC Awards, making him the most awarded player in international cricket history. He won the ODI Player of the Year award four times, in 2012, 2017, 2018, and 2023. He won the Cricketer of the Year award on two occasions, in 2017 and 2018. In 2018, he became the first player to win all three major ICC awards including Cricketer of the Year, ODI Player of the Year and Test Player of the Year in the same year. He was honored with the Spirit of Cricket Award in 2019 and given the Cricketer of the Decade and ODI Cricketer of the Decade in 2020. Kohli was named the Wisden Leading Cricketer in the World for three consecutive years.

Kohli has won the most Player of the Series and second-most Player of the Match awards to his name in all three formats combined. He was honoured with the Arjuna Award in 2013, the Padma Shri in 2017, and India's highest sporting honour, the Khel Ratna Award, in 2018. Time included him on its 100 most influential people in the world list in 2018. Kohli has been deemed one of the most commercially valuable athletes, with estimated earnings of ₹634 crore (equivalent to ₹692 crore or US$72 million in 2026) in 2022.

After winning the 2024 T20 World Cup being named Player of the Match award in the final, Kohli announced his retirement from T20Is. On 12 May 2025, at the age of 36, he announced his retirement from the Test cricket. He is married to actress Anushka Sharma, and they have two children.

Early life
Kohli was born on 5 November 1988 in New Delhi into a Punjabi Hindu family. His mother Saroj Kohli is a homemaker while his father Prem Nath Kohli worked as a criminal lawyer. He has an elder brother Vikas and an elder sister Bhawna. His formative years were spent in Uttam Nagar. His early education was at Vishal Bharti Public School.[3] As per his family, Kohli exhibited an early affinity for cricket as a 3-year-old. He would pick up a bat and request his father to bowl to him.[4] In 1998, the West Delhi Cricket Academy was created. In May, his father arranged for him to meet Rajkumar Sharma.[5] Upon the suggestion of their neighbours, Kohli's father considered enrolling his son in a professional cricket academy, as they believed his ability merited more than gully cricket.[6]

Kohli was unable to secure a place in the U-14 Delhi team, due to extraneous factors. His father reportedly received offers to relocate his son to influential clubs, which would ensure his selection, but he declined the proposals. Kohli eventually found his way into the U-15 team.[7] He received training at the academy and participated in matches at the Sumeet Dogra Academy located at Vasundhara Enclave.[8] To further his cricket career, he transferred to Saviour Convent School during his ninth grade.[6] On 18 December 2006, his father died due to a cerebral attack.[9] As per his mother, Kohli's demeanour shifted noticeably after his father's death. He took on cricket with newfound seriousness, prioritizing playing time and dedicating himself fully to the sport.[6] Kohli's family resided in Meera Bagh, Paschim Vihar until 2015, after which they relocated to Gurgaon.[10]

Youth career
Delhi team
Kohli's junior cricket career kicked off in October 2002 at the Luhnu Cricket Ground against Himachal Pradesh. His first half-century in domestic cricket happened at Feroze Shah Kotla, where he scored 70 runs against Haryana.[11] By the end of the season, he had amassed a total of 172 runs, emerging as the highest run-scorer for his team with an average of 34.40.[12] During the 2003–04 season of Polly Umrigar Trophy, Kohli was appointed the captain of the U-15 team.[12] He scored 54 runs in Delhi's victory over Himachal Pradesh. In the next fixture against Jammu and Kashmir, Kohli scored his maiden century with a score of 119. By the end of the season, he had a total of 390 runs at an average of 78, which included two centuries.[13] Towards the end of 2004, Kohli earned selection for the 2004–05 Vijay Merchant Trophy with the Delhi U-17 team.[12] In the four matches that he played, Kohli had a total of 470 runs, with his highest score being 251* runs. The team's coach, Ajit Chaudhary, lauded his performance and was particularly impressed with his temperament on the field.[14] He commenced the 2005–06 season with a score of 227 against Punjab. Following their victory over Uttar Pradesh in the quarter-finals, Delhi was scheduled to play against Baroda in the semi-finals. The team had high expectations from Kohli, who had promised his coach to finish the job. True to his word, Kohli went on to score 228 runs, leading Delhi to victory. The team later secured the tournament with a five-wicket win over Mumbai, where he contributed with a half-century in the first innings.[15] He ended as the highest run-scorer with a total of 757 runs from 7 matches, averaging 84.11.[16]

On 18 February 2006, Kohli made his debut in List A cricket, playing against Services in the Ranji One-Day Trophy, but he did not get the opportunity to bat during the match.[16] In 2006, Kohli got a spot in the state senior team. Subsequently, he made his first-class debut on 23 November 2006, during the opening match of the Ranji Trophy season against Tamil Nadu. However, his debut innings was a brief one, as he was dismissed after scoring ten runs.[17] In the subsequent match against former champions, Karnataka, Delhi found themselves trailing with a score of 130/5, with Kohli remaining unbeaten on 40 at the end of the day's play. That night, Kohli's father died. Despite the heart-wrenching news, Kohli returned to the match and continued to bat and scored 90 runs before he was dismissed.[18] Chetan Chauhan, the coach, was impressed by his determination and unwavering attitude in the face of adversity. Venkatesh Prasad lauded his crucial knock, which was executed in the midst of an emotional upheaval. After his dismissal, Kohli attended his father's funeral. His innings proved to be crucial for Delhi as they were able to avoid the follow-on. The team's captain, Mithun Manhas, praised Kohli for his performance, acknowledging its pivotal role in the team's success.[19]

Kohli's foray into T20 cricket first happened in April 2007, during the Inter-State T20 Championship, where he emerged as the top run-getter for his team with a tally of 179 runs at an average of 35.80.[20] In Sep 2008, Kohli played in Nissar Trophy against SNGPL. He emerged as the leading scorer for Delhi in both innings, registering 52 runs in the first innings and a towering 197 in the second. The match ultimately ended in a draw, SNGPL being declared the victors due to their lead in first innings.[21] In the 2009–10 Ranji Trophy season, Kohli returned to domestic cricket. During a match against Maharashtra, he opened the batting and scored 67 runs, helping Delhi to secure the bonus point required for victory.[22] Kohli's performance reinvigorated the competitive spirit of the domestic cricket circuit.

India U19 team
In July 2006, Kohli was selected in the India Under-19 squad on its tour of England. He averaged 105 in the three-match ODI series against England Under-19s, while also averaging 49 in the 3-match Test series. Following India U-19 success in both the ODI and Test series, the team's coach Lalchand Rajput noted Kohli's adeptness in facing both pace and spin bowling and expressed his admiration for his technical prowess.[23][24] In September, the U-19 team toured Pakistan. In the first Test match, Kohli scored 63 and 28 as India won by 271 runs against Pakistan Under-19s. In the 2nd match, he contributed 83 runs to India's victory by 240 runs and an innings. He concluded the tour with 80 runs in the final ODI game at Lahore.[25] In early 2007, Kohli was a part of the India U-19 team that toured New Zealand, where he scored 113 in the first Test match. The series ended in a draw. In the following month, the team travelled to Malaysia for a tri-series against England Under-19s and Sri Lanka Under-19s, where Kohli did not get many opportunities to bat. In July–August, India U-19 embarked on a tour for a tri-series against Sri Lanka Under-19s and Bangladesh Under-19s, where he did not score a half-century in any of the matches. He made a comeback with scores of 144 and an unbeaten 94 in the following Test series.[26]

Kohli came into the limelight in 2008 when he led the team to victory in the U-19 World Cup. He led the Indian squad and won the 2008 U-19 World Cup held in Malaysia.[27] He amassed 235 runs at an average of 47, ranking as the tournament's third-highest scorer and one of three cricketers to compile a century.[28] His century, a knock of 100 runs off 74 balls, versus the West Indies Under-19s in a group stage encounter, was lauded by ESPNcricinfo, as "the innings of the tournament." This innings paved the way for India's 50-run triumph and fetched Kohli the man of the match award.[29] Additionally, Kohli's all-round performance in the semi-final against New Zealand Under-19s, where he captured 2 wickets and contributed 43 runs in the run-chase, was core to India's victory.[30] In the championship match, Kohli managed a score of 19 against South Africa Under-19s and his contribution lead to the eventual 12-run win (via D/L method).[31]

In June 2008, Kohli and his U-19 teammates Pradeep Sangwan and Tanmay Srivastava were awarded the Border–Gavaskar scholarship. This scholarship, aimed at honing the skills of the chosen cricketers, provided an opportunity to train for six weeks at Cricket Australia's Centre of Excellence in Brisbane.[32] In a bid to identify potential talent for the senior team, Kohli was selected to represent India Emerging Players in the Emerging Players Tournament 2008. His finest performance in the tournament was against New Zealand Emerging Players, where he played a knock of 120 runs, leading India to a seven-wicket victory.[33] With an aggregate of 204 runs, Kohli's performances did not go unnoticed by the selectors who were observing his progress. He began his international cricket journey by joining the senior team in Colombo, having played 28 Under-19 ODIs and 12 Under-19 Tests.[34]

International career
Main article: Career of Virat Kohli
Kohli's international career began in August 2008 when the 19-year-old had a "surprise call-up" to the ODI squad for a tour of Sri Lanka.[35] He opened the batting due to injuries to senior players, scoring his first half-century in the fourth match.[36] After a brief stint with the India A team, he scored a century against a strong Australian bowling line-up in a tour match.[37] Despite an early BCCI contract, Kohli's place in the team was not secure. A turning point came in the 2009 Emerging Players Tournament in Australia, where he was the top run-scorer, leading his team to victory with a century in the final. This performance cemented his return to the national team.[38] He scored his maiden ODI century in December 2009 against Sri Lanka.[39] By early 2010, he became the third Indian to score two ODI centuries before turning 22.[40]

Kohli fielding during a match in December 2010
In 2010, Kohli was appointed vice-captain for a tri-series in Zimbabwe and became the then fastest Indian to score 1,000 ODI runs. After a dip in form during the 2010 Asia Cup, he solidified his position with consistent performances, finishing as India's leading ODI run-scorer for the year.[41] Kohli played a crucial role in India's 2011 World Cup victory, scoring a century on his debut and a 35 in the final.[42][43] Further made his Test debut in June 2011 against the West Indies, but struggled initially and was dropped.[44] He was recalled and eventually found his footing, scoring his maiden Test century in Adelaide in January 2012.[45] On 28 February 2012, during the Commonwealth Bank tri-series in Hobart, Kohli scored an unbeaten 133 runs from 86 balls against Sri Lanka, helping India chase 321 in 36.4 overs to secure a bonus-point victory and remain in contention for the tournament final.[46] and a career-best 183 against Pakistan in the 2012 Asia Cup, being the standout performances.[47][48]

By 2013, Kohli was a linchpin of the Indian batting line-up, particularly in run-chases.[49] He played a key role in India's 2013 Champions Trophy win[50] and was appointed captain for the first time during a tri-series in the West Indies, where he scored his first century as skipper.[51] He later established several records, including the fastest ODI century by an Indian.[52] After a difficult tour of England in 2014 where he averaged 13.4,[53] Kohli regained form and was named the full-time Test captain following MS Dhoni's retirement during the tour of Australia.[54] In his first series as permanent captain, he scored three centuries in his first three innings, totaling 692 runs, the most by an Indian batsman in a Test series in Australia.[55] He also remained consistent in the T20 format, earning the Man of the Tournament award at the 2014 ICC World Twenty20 for his 319 runs in the tournament.[56]

Kohli at Greenfield Stadium during match with West Indies
Kohli's form in the lead-up to the World Cup was not at his best, however after a strong start to the 2015 World Cup with a century against Pakistan,[57] Kohli's tournament ended with a score of 1 in the semi-final loss to Australia.[58] A subsequent dip in form was followed by his first Test series win as captain in Sri Lanka.[59] From 2016 to 2018, he entered a peak phase of his career.[60] In 2016, he was the Player of the Tournament at the ICC World T20.[61] He became the first batsman to score double centuries in four consecutive Test series and was appointed captain for the 2017 Champions Trophy, where India finished as runners-up.[62][63] This period saw him break numerous records, including becoming the fastest to 8,000, 10,000, and 11,000 ODI runs.[64][65] In 2018, he became the No. 1 ranked Test batsman and led India to first-ever Test series victory in Australia.[66] By 2019, he became India's most successful Test captain, holding the ICC Test Mace for three consecutive years.[67] He scored his 70th international century in November 2019, but this was followed by a prolonged lean patch.[68] From 2020 to 2022, Kohli struggled for runs and stepped down from the T20I, ODI, and Test captaincy in succession.[69]

Kohli's return to form began at the 2022 Asia Cup, where he scored his maiden T20I century, his first in any format in over 1,000 days.[70] He was the highest run-scorer at the 2022 T20 World Cup, playing an impactful innings of 82* against Pakistan.[71] His peak resurgence came at the 2023 World Cup on home soil where he was named the Player of the Tournament for scoring a record 765 runs in a single edition. During the tournament, he scored his 50th ODI hundred, surpassing Tendulkar's long-standing record.[72] In next year's T20 World Cup; Kohli had a lean tournament, however delivered a player of the match performance in the final, scoring 76 as India won the trophy. Following the victory, he announced his retirement from T20 Internationals.[73] In the 2025 Champions Trophy, Kohli was instrumental in India's victory, scoring a century and becoming the fastest to 14,000 ODI runs.[74] India later secured the title. On 12 May 2025, after poor Border-Gavaskar Trophy performances he announced that the Test-series would be his last, marking his retirement from Test cricket.[75]

Virat Kohli scored his 54th ODI century against New Zealand in the third ODI at Indore, reaching the milestone in 91 balls with eight fours and two sixes while chasing a target of 337. With this innings, he became the leading century-maker against New Zealand with seven hundreds, surpassing Ricky Ponting and Virender Sehwag (six each), and Sachin Tendulkar and Sanath Jayasuriya (five each). Kohli also became the highest run-scorer batting at number three. The century was his 85th in international cricket and his 41st on home soil.[76]
